name: SearXNG
purpose: Self-hosted privacy-respecting metasearch engine that queries dozens of upstream engines and aggregates the results, with no user profiling and configurable engine selection.
journalism_use_case: Run queries across dozens of engines from one self-hosted instance, compare result sets to see what each engine suppresses or elevates, and avoid personalised results during research — which matters because a logged-in Google session quietly shapes what an investigation finds.
pros: Eliminates search personalisation as a confounder, so two reporters researching the same subject see the same thing and results are reproducible enough to describe in a methodology note
Querying many engines at once routinely surfaces results that a single engine buries — the practical core of search-based OSINT
Largest and most active community in this subcategory (39,634 stars, pushed 2026-11-17), so engine-scraper breakage gets fixed quickly, which is the dominant failure mode here
Self-hosting keeps query logs on your own infrastructure instead of with a search provider — a real operational-security gain when your queries reveal an investigation
cons: Result completeness varies by engine health: scrapers break, engines rate-limit, and an empty result set can mean 'nothing found' or 'engine broken' with no clear distinction
No persistent archiving of results, so you must capture anything you intend to cite with a separate tool

Queries still leave your instance to upstream engines, so the engines see the query (from your server's IP) even though they do not see a user profile — self-hosting changes who correlates, not whether queries are visible
AGPL-3.0 network copyleft applies if you modify and expose an instance to others; 208 open issues reflects constant engine maintenance
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. The checkable signals are strong: 39,634 stars, 208 open issues and same-day commits on 2026-11-17 — the open-issue count is characteristic of a project whose scrapers constantly need repair as engines change. Widely recommended in OSINT training material.
assessment: Adopt and self-host — this is the cheapest meaningful improvement to search-based research, and the de-personalisation property alone justifies it. For your profile two configuration points matter: run it behind your own network so the upstream engines see your server rather than a reporter's home connection, and set an explicit expectation that an engine returning nothing may be broken, not empty. Pair with SingleFile or Scoop to preserve anything you will cite.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, no release objects (continuous-delivery model), 39,634 stars, 208 open issues. Daily commits from a large community; the absence of versioned releases is a deliberate rolling-release choice rather than a maintenance gap.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0: if you modify SearXNG and offer it over a network, you must publish your modified source. Running it unmodified for your newsroom carries no obligation. Some upstream engines' terms of service prohibit automated querying — a terms question separate from the licence.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure estimate: one small VM or container; some engines require API keys with their own quotas and costs (not priced here). Operating effort is low but non-zero — expect occasional engine breakage to investigate.
privacy: Self-hosting keeps query logs local and removes profiling. The residual exposure is real and should be understood: queries are forwarded to upstream engines from your instance's IP, so a sustained investigation produces a visible query pattern attributable to your organisation's address. Consider routing through Tor or a dedicated egress if that matters.
alternatives: 4get for a lighter-weight self-hosted metasearch
LibreY where even SearXNG is more than you want to operate
Marginalia Search for a deliberately non-commercial index that surfaces different material

name: 4get
purpose: Lightweight PHP metasearch proxy that queries multiple upstream engines without requiring JavaScript or accounts, returning plain aggregated results.
journalism_use_case: Query several engines without logging in or running JavaScript, and compare how different engines rank the same target — useful on a hardened or low-bandwidth machine where a full SearXNG deployment or a JavaScript-heavy interface is impractical.
pros: No JavaScript required, which makes it usable from a locked-down browser, a text browser or a minimal field device — a genuine niche that SearXNG does not fill as well
Very small PHP deployment, so it runs on almost anything including shared hosting
Verified actively developed: the project's own forge shows commits dated 2026-11-15, so despite being off GitHub it is current
AGPL-3.0-only, so the privacy-preserving intent is legally reinforced for anyone redeploying it
cons: Not on GitHub but on a self-hosted forge, which means no GitHub API metadata, no dependency-scanner integration, and a smaller contributor pool — assessment depends on reading that forge directly
Scraper breakage is routine and the smaller contributor base means slower repair than SearXNG
Engine coverage and result quality are below SearXNG's
Using someone else's public 4get instance means the operator sees your queries — the same caveat as any shared metasearch, and more acute with a small single-maintainer project
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Verified directly from the project's forge on 2026-11-17: the master branch commit list shows commits dated 2026-11-15, confirming current development. No star or issue metrics are available because the project is not on GitHub, so community-size signals cannot be reported.
assessment: A useful second option rather than a primary tool: I would deploy SearXNG as the newsroom instance and keep 4get in mind for the specific case of a no-JavaScript or very constrained client. For media-in-exile contexts that constraint is not hypothetical — a reporter on a hardened machine or a censored connection may genuinely need a text-only search path. Verify its liveness on the forge rather than assuming, since no GitHub signals exist.
maintenance_evidence: Project forge (git.lolcat.ca/lolcat/4get) read directly on 2026-11-17: master-branch commits dated 2026-11-15. HTTP 200 and a populated commit list. No GitHub metadata exists for this project, so star counts, issue counts and release objects are unavailable — classification rests on commit recency from the authoritative source.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0-only network copyleft: modifying and exposing an instance obliges source publication. Upstream engines' terms on automated querying apply separately.
costs: No fee. Minimal PHP host. Negligible infrastructure.
privacy: Your own instance proxies queries to upstream engines, so those engines see your server's IP. Using a public instance means the operator sees your queries — avoid public instances for investigative searches.
alternatives: SearXNG as the primary self-hosted metasearch
LibreY as another lightweight PHP option
Direct engine queries through Tor Browser when the priority is unlinkability rather than aggregation

name: LibreY
purpose: Lightweight self-hosted metasearch front end in PHP that proxies queries to several upstream engines and aggregates results, with optional instance federation.
journalism_use_case: Lightweight self-hosted meta-search for quick multi-engine checks when a full SearXNG deployment is overkill — for instance a per-investigation throwaway instance on cheap hosting, kept separate from the newsroom's main search path.
pros: Very small footprint: a PHP host is enough, so standing up a disposable instance for one investigation is realistic
Keeps query logs off commercial search providers in the same way SearXNG does, at a fraction of the operational weight
AGPL-3.0, so redeployments inherit the same openness obligation
cons: Smaller engine coverage and a slower cadence than SearXNG — last push 2026-06-10, five months before this survey
Small community (328 stars, 25 open issues), so scraper breakage may persist longer than in SearXNG
No release objects at all, so there is no version to pin and upgrades mean tracking the default branch
PHP deployment is a different operational idiom from the rest of a typical Python/TypeScript newsroom stack
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 328 stars with 25 open issues, no releases, last push 2026-06-10. Positioned by its own documentation as a lighter alternative to SearXNG, which matches the metadata picture.
assessment: Hard to justify over SearXNG for a primary instance, given SearXNG's much faster scraper repair and larger engine set. Where LibreY earns consideration is the disposable-instance pattern: cheap, fast to deploy, and discardable after an investigation — which has a genuine operational-security logic if you do not want all of an investigation's queries traceable to one long-lived server. Treat as a secondary option and check its liveness before relying on it.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-06-10, no releases or tags, 328 stars, 25 open issues. Five months quiet. For a metasearch project — where upstream engines change constantly — five months of silence is more concerning than it would be for a stable library, so this classification is cautious rather than generous.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0 network copyleft on modified public instances. Upstream engine terms apply separately.
costs: No fee. A minimal PHP host; negligible.
privacy: Queries are proxied to upstream engines from your instance. Self-hosting keeps logs local; a public instance exposes your queries to its operator.
alternatives: SearXNG — the recommended primary choice
4get for a no-JavaScript lightweight option with more recent commits
Tor Browser plus direct engine queries for unlinkability

name: Whoogle Search
purpose: Self-hosted, ad-free, JavaScript-free front end that proxied Google search results without cookies or tracking.
journalism_use_case: Historically used to query Google without a personalised session; now mainly a reference for why self-hosted Google front-ends are no longer viable, which is itself a useful fact when planning a research stack.
pros: Solved a real problem well while it worked: Google results without a session, cookies or personalisation
MIT licensed with a clean, small codebase worth reading if you are building any search proxy
Large user base at archival (11,551 stars) with essentially no open issues, indicating it was finished rather than neglected
cons: ARCHIVED: GitHub API confirms archived=true, last push 2026-08-14 — read-only, no further development
Depends on a Google scraping path that Google has closed, so the core function is broken rather than merely unmaintained
The documented fallback is the paid Google Custom Search API (100 free queries per day, then paid), which defeats the original purpose and introduces a vendor dependency
Any fork inherits the same blocked scraping path, so forking does not solve the problem
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The decisive documented facts: archived=true per the GitHub API on 2026-11-17, and the project's own documentation of the Google Custom Search API fallback (100 free queries/day then paid) as the alternative to the blocked scraping path. 11,551 stars, 1 open issue, release v1.2.4 (2026-04-15).
assessment: Reference only, and a clear data point for your planning: direct Google access is no longer available to self-hosted tooling, so a research stack must be built on metasearch across accessible engines (SearXNG), on independent indexes (Marginalia, YaCy), or on paid API access. Anyone proposing a Google-scraping component in 2026 should be shown this entry. Do not deploy.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=true, pushed_at 2026-08-14, latest release v1.2.4 (2026-04-15), 11,551 stars, 1 open issue. Archived by the maintainer, and the underlying capability is blocked upstream by Google — both code and function are dead.
licence_restrictions: None, but the code is frozen and non-functional for its primary purpose.
costs: No fee. The viable fallback path (Google Custom Search API) is a paid dependency beyond 100 free queries per day — rates not verified in this survey.
privacy: Queries were proxied from your instance to Google. With the Custom Search API fallback, queries go to Google under an API key tied to your account — a weaker privacy position than the original design.
alternatives: SearXNG — the maintained replacement for the general need
Marginalia Search or YaCy for independent indexes not dependent on Google
Paid Google Custom Search API if Google results are genuinely required, accepting the cost and the account linkage
blockers: Archived; the Google scraping path it depends on is closed

name: Marginalia Search
purpose: Independent search engine with its own crawler and index that deliberately de-prioritises commercial content, surfacing small, text-heavy, non-commercial websites.
journalism_use_case: Surface obscure personal pages, forums and old sites that mainstream engines suppress — useful for finding early traces of a person or organisation, the self-published page from 2009, or the small forum where a subject once posted under their own name.
pros: A genuinely independent index, not a proxy over Google or Bing, so it finds material the major engines have dropped or never ranked — the single most useful property for background research on an individual
The deliberate anti-commercial ranking bias is the feature: it inverts the SEO filter that buries exactly the amateur and archival pages an investigation wants
Self-hostable in principle (AGPL-3.0), so a newsroom could run its own index over chosen corpora
Actively developed (pushed 2026-11-16) by a maintainer with a sustained multi-year commitment
cons: Deliberately partial index: it is not a Google replacement and will miss mainstream coverage entirely, so it complements rather than substitutes
Self-hosting requires large storage and CPU for the index — realistically out of reach for most newsrooms, so in practice you use the public instance
Release metadata is stale (v24.10.0 from 2024-10-14) and GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION, so the AGPL-3.0 label rests on project documentation rather than a detected licence file
Queries to the public instance go to its operator; the operator is a small independent project rather than an organisation with a formal privacy programme
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 2,240 stars with 31 open issues, pushed 2026-11-16, release object v24.10.0 (2024-10-14), SPDX NOASSERTION. Marginalia has a strong reputation among researchers for surfacing non-commercial web content, reflected in its community following.
assessment: Worth adding to your standard research routine specifically for person and organisation background, where its index composition is a real advantage over mainstream search. Use the public instance and treat the operator as a third party who sees your queries — for a sensitive subject, query through Tor. Do not plan to self-host unless you have serious storage to spare; the public instance is the practical product.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v24.10.0 (2024-10-14), SPDX NOASSERTION, 2,240 stars, 31 open issues. Current commits and a continuously operated public service; the stale release object reflects a service-first rather than release-first project.
licence: AGPL-3.0 (per project documentation; GitHub API reports NOASSERTION)
model_or_data_licence: The index is the project's own crawl; crawled content belongs to the original publishers.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0 network copyleft would apply to a modified self-hosted instance. Confirm the licence file before forking, given the SPDX gap.
costs: Free to use the public instance. Self-hosting requires large storage and CPU for crawling and indexing — a substantial infrastructure commitment, not quantified here because it depends entirely on index scope.
privacy: Queries to the public instance go to the operator; self-hosting keeps everything local. No personalisation or profiling is applied, but the operator is a small project rather than an institution — route sensitive queries through Tor.
alternatives: SearXNG to query many engines including, where available, independent ones
YaCy for a self-hosted index over a defined set of target sites
Internet Archive full-text search for historical web material

name: YaCy
purpose: Peer-to-peer search engine that crawls and indexes websites locally, usable as a standalone private index or federated with other peers.
journalism_use_case: Build a private searchable index over a defined set of target sites — ministries, forums, company websites — for repeatable full-text investigation, so a query runs against your own crawl rather than against whatever a commercial engine currently chooses to show.
pros: A private index over chosen sites is qualitatively different from search: results are reproducible, complete within your crawl, and unaffected by engine ranking changes — which makes 'this phrase appears nowhere on the ministry's site' a statement you can actually support
Crawled content stays local, so your research targets are not disclosed to any search provider
Mature, long-lived project still receiving commits (pushed 2026-11-03) under GPL-2.0-or-later
Can run in standalone mode with no peer-to-peer participation, keeping the deployment self-contained
cons: Heavy resource use: a serious index needs substantial disk and RAM, and the Java stack is not light
Relevance ranking is noticeably weaker than commercial engines, so finding things in a large index takes more query craft
Dated UI and 248 open issues, with no release objects (latest tag Release_1.941) and SPDX NOASSERTION despite the GPL licence — assessment requires reading the repository rather than its metadata
P2P mode shares index fragments with other peers, which would disclose aspects of your crawl — this must be deliberately disabled for investigative use
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 4,110 stars with 248 open issues, last push 2026-11-03, no release objects, latest tag Release_1.941, SPDX NOASSERTION. A long-running community project with a large accumulated backlog.
assessment: Niche but genuinely valuable for one task: exhaustive, reproducible search over a bounded set of sites you care about. For your profile I would deploy it in standalone mode (P2P off, explicitly verified) over the ministries, registries and company sites relevant to a long-running beat, and treat it as an evidentiary instrument rather than a discovery one. If you only need discovery, SearXNG is far less work.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-03, no release objects, latest tag Release_1.941, 4,110 stars, 248 open issues. Commits continue but the large backlog and informal release process indicate a mature community project running at low velocity rather than active development.
model_or_data_licence: Your crawl contains third-party content subject to the original publishers' rights.
licence_restrictions: GPL-2.0-or-later on the software. Crawling may engage target sites' terms of service — a separate consideration from the licence.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure estimate: a JVM host with substantial disk for the index — a few hundred GB for a meaningful multi-site crawl, scaling with scope. Assumptions: standalone mode, text-focused index.
privacy: Crawled content is stored locally and queries never leave your machine in standalone mode — the strongest privacy position in this subcategory. P2P mode shares index fragments with other peers and must be disabled for investigative work. Note that your crawler's requests are visible to the target sites.
alternatives: Apache Solr plus your own crawler (Heritrix, browsertrix-crawler) for more control and better ranking
SearXNG for discovery rather than exhaustive search
Marginalia Search where you want someone else's independent index
blockers: P2P mode would disclose index fragments — must be explicitly disabled

name: pagodo
purpose: Tool that scraped the Google Hacking Database for dork patterns and ran them against Google to find exposed files, directories and interfaces on a target domain.
journalism_use_case: Reference implementation of bulk dorking workflows; its GHDB scraper still documents dork syntax that remains useful for manual searching — for example finding exposed procurement spreadsheets or misconfigured document directories on a target's domain.
pros: The GHDB dork catalogue it scrapes remains a genuinely useful reference for manual search syntax, independent of the automation
Clean, readable implementation of the dorking workflow, with GPL-3.0 licensing
Had a long run as the standard tool in this niche, so understanding it explains most dorking tooling you will encounter
cons: ARCHIVED: the GitHub API confirms archived=true as of this survey, with the final release v2.8.0 on 2026-11-01 — the maintainer wound it down rather than abandoning it quietly
Automated Google dorking is broadly non-functional as of late 2026 because of Google's anti-scraping measures, so the core capability no longer works regardless of code quality
Dork queries issued directly to Google from your IP are a visible, attributable pattern — and in an investigation that pattern can be linked to you
Depends on GHDB (Offensive Security), a third-party catalogue whose availability and terms you do not control
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Decisive documented facts: archived=true per the GitHub API on 2026-11-17 with a final release v2.8.0 (2026-11-01); 3,418 stars with 0 open issues. The practical collapse of automated Google dorking in 2026 is corroborated by the same pattern in dorks_hunter and Whoogle.
assessment: Reference only. The honest conclusion for your work is that dorking is now a manual technique: keep the GHDB syntax patterns to hand and run them by hand through SearXNG or directly, accepting low volume. Do not build a pipeline on automated dorking — it will fail and, worse, will fail intermittently in ways that look like 'nothing found'. If exposed-file discovery matters, katana or a targeted crawl of the domain is the reliable substitute.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=true, pushed_at 2026-11-01, latest release v2.8.0 (2026-11-01), 3,418 stars, 0 open issues. Archived with a final release — an orderly wind-down. The upstream capability (Google scraping) is independently blocked.
model_or_data_licence: The GHDB dork catalogue is maintained by Offensive Security under its own terms, not covered by pagodo's licence.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0 on the code. GHDB content terms are separate. Automated querying breaches Google's terms of service — a terms rather than licence issue, but a real one.
costs: No fee. Not operable for its primary purpose.
privacy: Dork queries were issued directly to Google from your IP — a highly visible and attributable pattern. Anyone reviving this approach should consider that the search provider can profile the campaign.
alternatives: Manual dorking through SearXNG at low volume
katana for crawling a target domain to enumerate files and paths directly
uncover for exposed-infrastructure discovery via scan databases (paid API keys)
blockers: Archived; automated Google dorking is non-functional as of late 2026

name: dorks_hunter
purpose: Script that runs a curated set of Google dork queries against a target domain to find exposed documents, configuration files, login panels and third-party exposures.
journalism_use_case: One of the few dorking helpers still receiving commits after pagodo's archival, for quick exposed-file discovery on a domain — for example surfacing a council's inadvertently public document directory.
pros: Still receiving commits (pushed 2026-07-14) after the archival of pagodo, so it is the most current option in a collapsing niche
Curated dork set is narrower and more practical than the full GHDB, which makes manual review of results feasible
Simple enough to read in full and adapt, which is how it should be used given the reliability problem
cons: UNLICENSED: the GitHub API reports no detected licence and session-1 inspection found none, so reuse and redistribution are legally unresolved
Reliability is bounded by Google's 2026 anti-scraping changes, the same constraint that killed pagodo — expect intermittent and silent failure
Release metadata is effectively absent (v1.0 from 2022-08-03 against current commits), so there is no meaningful version to pin
Dork queries are issued to Google from your IP, producing an attributable pattern
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: no licence detected by the GitHub API (verified session 1, retained); 350 stars with 0 open issues; last push 2026-07-14; release v1.0 dated 2022-08-03. The zero-issue count on a scraping tool in 2026 more likely reflects an unattended tracker than a flawless tool.
assessment: Not something I would depend on: unlicensed and built on a capability Google has largely closed. Read the dork list, use the patterns manually, and if exposed-document discovery matters to a beat, build it on a direct crawl (katana, Photon) which is both lawful under the target's robots posture and reliable. The licence gap alone should keep it out of any newsroom codebase.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-07-14, latest release v1.0 (2022-08-03), no detected licence, 350 stars, 0 open issues. Four months since last push on a script-sized project; activity continues but the upstream capability is degraded, which matters more than cadence here.
licence: NOT CONFIRMED — no licence detected by the GitHub API and no LICENSE file found
licence_restrictions: Unresolved: without a licence, you have no granted rights to copy, modify or redistribute. Do not vendor it into a newsroom codebase. Automated Google querying also breaches Google's terms.
costs: No fee. Low value per unit of effort given reliability problems.
privacy: Dork queries are issued to Google from your IP, producing a visible and attributable pattern tied to your investigation.
alternatives: Manual dorking through SearXNG
katana or Photon for direct enumeration of a target domain
uncover for exposed-service discovery via scan-database APIs
blockers: Automated Google dorking degraded by anti-scraping measures

name: Metabigor
purpose: Go tool that gathers organisational internet footprint data — IP netblocks, ASNs, related hosts, certificate and scan data — from public sources without requiring API keys for its core functions.
journalism_use_case: Quickly map an organisation's internet footprint (netblocks, ASNs, related hosts) from public sources before deeper investigation — for example establishing which IP ranges a surveillance vendor controls before looking at what runs on them.
pros: Works without paid API keys for core functions, which distinguishes it from uncover and makes it usable without a budget or vendor account
ASN and netblock mapping is the right first step in infrastructure investigation and is tedious to do by hand
MIT licensed, single Go binary, actively released (v2.2.0, 2026-08-08) with a near-empty issue tracker (2 open)
cons: Infrastructure-oriented rather than social-media oriented, so it answers only one class of question
Output needs manual validation: public ASN and netblock attribution is frequently stale or wrong, and publishing an incorrect 'company X controls this range' claim is a real risk
Queries are sent from your host to third-party public services, so those services see your targets
Last push 2026-08-08 — three months before this survey, with no activity since the release
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 1,871 stars with only 2 open issues, release v2.2.0 on 2026-08-08 (same-day push). The very low issue count suggests either good triage or light use; with 1,871 stars the former is more likely.
assessment: A good first instrument for the surveillance-infrastructure investigations in the B2 part of your work: cheap, no vendor account, and it narrows the search space fast. The discipline required is verification — confirm netblock ownership against RIR records (RIPE, ARIN) before any published claim, because public attribution data lags reality by months. Pair with uncover or direct certificate-transparency queries for what is actually running.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-08-08, latest release v2.2.0 published the same day, 1,871 stars, 2 open issues. Three months since last activity; a small, feature-complete Go tool with a clean tracker. Not classified actively maintained because there is no activity in the last quarter.
model_or_data_licence: n/a — queries third-party public services whose own terms apply.
licence_restrictions: None material for the code. The third-party services it queries have their own terms on automated access.
costs: No fee and no required API keys for core functions — unusual and valuable in this category. Negligible compute.
privacy: Queries are sent from your host to third-party public services, which therefore learn which organisations you are mapping. Use a dedicated egress or Tor where the target should not learn of your interest.
alternatives: uncover for scan-database queries (paid API keys, broader data)
amass or subfinder for subdomain-focused enumeration
Direct RIR (RIPE/ARIN) and certificate-transparency queries for authoritative ownership data
